analysis.one_liner: Requires cancer-warning labels on food treated with carcinogenic pesticides and bans unsafe pesticide limits for children.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 1995 and referred to the House Commerce Committee and its Health and Environment Subcommittee, but never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required food labels to state when pesticides containing known or probable human carcinogens were applied to the food, giving shoppers that information at the store. It would also have barred the EPA from setting pesticide residue limits it determined could cause serious health effects in children, breast cancer, or serious reproductive disorders. The bill never moved past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers, who would see a plain-language notice when foods carried residues of pesticides classified as known or probable human carcinogens; children and pregnant women, since the EPA could no longer set residue limits it judged capable of causing cancer, damage to developing neurological, immune, or reproductive systems, breast cancer, or serious reproductive disorders [S2][S3]. The bill directed the EPA to follow the National Research Council's 1993 report on pesticides in the diets of infants and children [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food shoppers, children, and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Requires a label notice reading 'Pesticides Containing Known or Probable Human Carcinogens Have Been Applied to This Food' on any food treated with such pesticides, so shoppers can see it before buying.

Prohibits the EPA from setting a pesticide residue tolerance if dietary exposure under that tolerance is reasonably anticipated to cause serious adverse health effects in any child, including cancer or damage to developing neurological, immune, or reproductive systems.

Prohibits residue tolerances the EPA determines could cause breast cancer or serious reproductive disorders in any person, and directs the agency to implement the National Research Council's 1993 recommendations on pesticides in infants' and children's diets.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers, whose products could lose EPA residue approvals or carry a cancer warning on the food they were used on; farmers and food companies, who would bear labeling changes and might lose access to some pesticides [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: A blanket warning label on foods could alarm shoppers without telling them whether the residue levels actually posed a meaningful risk — a 'known or probable human carcinogen' designation reflects hazard evidence, not the dose on the food.

Banning tolerances the EPA 'reasonably anticipated' to affect any child could remove widely used pest-control tools, raising costs for farmers and potentially food prices, with limited documented offsetting benefit in the bill itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered shoppers direct information about carcinogenic pesticide residues and added a child-protective standard for residue limits, which is a real gain for families. The costs fell on pesticide makers and farmers, and the blunt label warning plus the strict 'any child' standard could have overcorrected, stamping warnings on foods at residue levels that may pose little risk. On balance it was a consumer-protection measure whose burden fell on a specific industry rather than on ordinary households.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Commerce Committee, which passed it down to a subcommittee that never acted, and the bill died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the Pesticide Safety and Right-to-Know Act of 1995 on June 7, 1995, with two Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce the same day, and on June 19, 1995 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment.
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — is recorded before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers and food producers were better off, since no labeling requirement or new child-health restrictions on residue limits ever took effect; shoppers got no new right to know.

for.name: Rep. Henry A. Waxman
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member

for.name: Two House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors.

against.name: House Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Thomas Bliley)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never reported it out; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: House Agriculture and food and pesticide industries
against.what_they_did: The bill targeted pesticide residue tolerances and mandatory cancer labels on food, industries that broadly opposed stricter pesticide rules in this era; no formal position from them appears in the provided record.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats and the House never voted, so no roll call shows where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill could have removed EPA residue tolerances for products the agency determined could harm children, cause breast cancer, or cause reproductive disorders, shrinking the market for those pesticides [S2][S3]. Mandatory carcinogen warning labels on treated food also added reputational and labeling costs.

Farmers could have lost access to effective pesticides and food companies would have faced new label requirements, but nothing in the bill restricted their sales outright [S2][S3]. Their costs rose while consumers gained information.
